## About This Episode

In this episode, Cecep Mustafa examines Japan's civil conciliation infrastructure (Minji Chōtei) under the Civil Conciliation Act of 1951 (Act No. 222 of 1951) and evaluates its strategic value for court-annexed mediation reform in Indonesia. He explores how Japan utilizes specialized multi-member Conciliation Committees (Chōtei Iinkai) and early issue-sorting (sōten seiri) to structure disputes and facilitate negotiated settlements. The episode examines reported settlement performance, differences across court systems, and the institutional mechanisms that contribute to effective court-connected conciliation. Cecep Mustafa then analyzes potential operational bottlenecks in single-mediator models under Supreme Court Regulation (PERMA) No. 1 of 2016 and presents a structured 30-60-90 day pilot framework for Indonesian courts. The proposed approach adapts relevant Japanese institutional practices while emphasizing multidisciplinary expertise, early issue identification, settlement quality, measurable outcomes, and sustainable court-annexed mediation reform.

## Listen to the Episode

Building Effective Court Mediation: Japan's Civil Conciliation Model for Judicial Reform

## Key Topics

Japan Civil Conciliation, Minji Chōtei, Conciliation Committees, Court Annexed Mediation, Issue Sorting, PERMA 1 2016, PERMA 3 2022, Judicial Reform.

## Why This Topic Matters

Court-annexed mediation operates at the intersection of judicial administration and alternative dispute resolution. Its primary goals are reducing court backlogs, lowering litigation costs, and delivering sustainable dispute outcomes. In many jurisdictions, mandating mediation as a compulsory procedural gatekeeper fails to generate meaningful settlement when incentives, neutral skill sets, and attorney behaviors remain tied to adversarial litigation strategies. Analyzing Japan's high-performing conciliation framework provides actionable insights for transitioning court mediation from a routine formalistic hurdle into an effective, evaluative-facilitative dispute resolution mechanism.

## Japan Perspective

Japan's civil conciliation system (Minji Chōtei) is governed by the Civil Conciliation Act of 1951 (Act No. 222 of 1951). Historically rooted in dispute resolution practices emphasizing social harmony (wa), the system is built around specialized Conciliation Committees (Chōtei Iinkai). Each committee consists of one presiding Conciliation Judge (Chōtei Kan-an) and two or more lay Conciliation Commissioners (Chōtei Iin) appointed by the Supreme Court of Japan. Lay commissioners are selected from civil society and include attorneys, accountants, architects, engineers, medical specialists, and experienced corporate executives.

Procedurally, Japanese conciliation integrates early issue-sorting (sōten seiri) to narrow contested facts before settlement evaluations begin. Under Article 34 of Act No. 222, non-appearance without valid cause is punishable by administrative fines. When conciliation yields an agreement, Article 16 establishes that terms recorded in an official Conciliation Record (Chōtei Toshosho) carry immediate executory force equivalent to a final judicial judgment.

Empirically, Japanese civil conciliation consistently achieves high settlement rates. Official Supreme Court statistics from 2022 show that Minji Chōtei handled 33,934 national cases with an overall success rate exceeding 50 percent. Summary Court civil conciliation achieved settlement rates between 50 percent and 55 percent across 25,789 cases, while District Court conciliation achieved rates between 45 percent and 50 percent across 8,145 cases.

Technological integration has further streamlined these proceedings. Under the Code of Civil Procedure amendments (Act No. 48 of 2022) and the 2023 Integration Act (Act No. 53 of 2023), Japan established a full digital transition. This includes mandatory e-filing for licensed attorneys via the Supreme Court mints platform, centralized e-case management, and widespread use of web-conferencing software for preparatory hearings and conciliation sessions.

## Comparative Perspective

Comparative analysis reveals both shared normative goals and key structural divergences between Indonesia and Japan.

Both legal systems recognize court-connected mediation as an essential tool to manage caseloads and preserve social relationships. Indonesian mediation draws cultural legitimacy from the constitutional principles of Pancasila and the customary governance philosophy of Musyawarah Mufakat (deliberative consensus). Both jurisdictions assign full executory force to mediated agreements: Settlement Deeds (Akta Dading) in Indonesia under PERMA No. 1 of 2016 and Conciliation Records (Chōtei Toshosho) in Japan under Act No. 222 of 1951. Both have also established frameworks for electronic proceedings: PERMA No. 3 of 2022 in Indonesia and Act No. 48 of 2022 in Japan.

However, operational architectures differ significantly. Indonesia relies on a single mediator (either an active judge mediator or an external non-judge mediator certified via a 40-hour course) operating within a strict 30-calendar-day window. Under Article 7 of PERMA 1/2016, judges can declare lawsuits inadmissible (Niet Ontvankelijk Verklaard / NO) and impose cost orders for bad-faith participation (tidak beriktikad baik), though trial judges rarely enforce these sanctions in practice. In contrast, Japan uses multi-member expert committees, flexible timeframes structured around issue-sorting rounds (sōten seiri), and allows direct pre-litigation conciliation filings or ex officio court transfers.

These structural differences produce contrasting empirical outcomes:

In Indonesia, nationwide settlement rates in general civil litigation at District Courts (Pengadilan Negeri) remain between 6.8 percent and 7.42 percent (recording a 7.42 percent success rate across 18,347 cases in 2022). Religious Courts (Pengadilan Agama) achieve higher performance with a 39.85 percent national settlement rate across 63,312 cases in 2023, driven primarily by family disputes such as divorce and child custody. Significant local performance variations exist: Rangkasbitung Religious Court achieved over 61 percent success using active judge mediators, whereas Tangerang Religious Court recorded 7.04 percent success relying on uncompensated external non-judge mediators, and Sangatta Religious Court recorded 9.02 percent in contested divorce cases between 2022 and 2024.

In Japan, civil conciliation maintains consistent settlement rates above 50 percent across summary and district courts nationwide.

The primary driver of this disparity is how neutral authority and expertise are structured. In Indonesia, active judge mediators face heavy trial dockets, leaving limited time for individual mediation sessions. External non-judge mediators offer domain expertise but lack public court budget allocations to cover their fees, making them dependent on voluntary party fees and causing high roster attrition. Litigants often perceive non-judge mediators as lacking formal authority. In Japan, the Conciliation Committee combines judicial authority directly with specialized private-sector technical analysis, dividing analytical duties effectively across the panel.

Observe → Understand → Compare → Adapt → Pilot → Improve

The pathway for adapting Japanese institutional insights into Indonesian court reform follows a six-stage methodology:

Observe: Identify operational bottlenecks in Indonesia's single-mediator model, including low District Court settlement rates (7.42 percent) and resource deficits for external mediators.

Understand: Recognize that Japan's high conciliation settlement rates (>50 percent) stem from deliberate structural design choices, multidisciplinary panel composition, and early issue-sorting rather than cultural factors alone.

Compare: Contrast Indonesia's 30-day single-mediator gatekeeping rule under PERMA 1/2016 against Japan's multi-member evaluative-facilitative committees under Act No. 222 of 1951.

Adapt: Formulate specific regulatory proposals for Indonesia:

Amend PERMA 1/2016 to create Tripartite Conciliation Panels (1 Judge Mediator + 2 Certified Non-Judge Specialist Commissioners) for complex civil, land, and commercial disputes.

Codify a mandatory 10-day Issue-Sorting and Assessment Phase (Tahap Formulasi & Evaluasi Sengketa) to provide non-binding preliminary evaluations.

Enact a Joint Ministerial Decree (Surat Keputusan Bersama / SKB) between the Supreme Court, Ministry of Law, and Ministry of Finance to establish dedicated public funding and per-case honoraria for non-judge mediators.

Upgrade digital mediation capabilities under PERMA 3/2022 with secure digital evidence rooms, virtual caucuses, and electronic signature validation.

Pilot: Execute a 90-day pilot program across four representative courts: PN Jakarta Selatan (General Civil), PA Jakarta Selatan (Family/Sharia), PN Surabaya (Commercial/Land), and PA Sleman (Family/Local Wisdom).

Improve: Evaluate pilot outcomes against empirical benchmarks (target District Court settlement >=25 percent, Religious Court settlement >=55 percent, settlement duration <=18 calendar days, non-judge allocation >=45 percent, bad-faith penalty enforcement 100 percent) to refine regulations prior to national deployment.

## Judicial Knowledge Takeaways

Multidisciplinary Panels Enhance Authority and Evaluation: Combining judicial authority with private-sector technical expertise resolves domain knowledge gaps and prevents mediation sessions from becoming superficial procedural formalities.

Early Issue-Sorting Drives Settlement Realism: Introducing a structured issue-sorting phase (sōten seiri) narrows contested facts early, giving parties a clear evidentiary basis for realistic settlement evaluations.

Dedicated Public Funding Is Essential for Neutral Roster Retention: Court-annexed mediation cannot rely on voluntary party fees to compensate non-judge neutrals. Securing state budget line items is necessary to maintain professionalized rosters and protect lower-income litigants.

Judicial Authority Must Integrate into Mediation Workflows: Litigants engage more actively in negotiations when presiding judicial neutrals actively oversee procedural structure and enforce good-faith participation rules.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is the statutory foundation of civil conciliation in Japan? A: Civil conciliation in Japan (Minji Chōtei) is governed by the Civil Conciliation Act of 1951 (Act No. 222 of 1951), supplemented by the Code of Civil Procedure and recent digital court transformation statutes (Act No. 48 of 2022).

Q: How do settlement rates compare between Indonesian District Courts and Japanese Civil Conciliation? A: Indonesian District Courts record nationwide mediation settlement rates between 6.8 percent and 7.42 percent. Japanese Civil Conciliation consistently achieves nationwide settlement rates exceeding 50 percent across both Summary Courts and District Courts.

Q: How is a Japanese Conciliation Committee (Chōtei Iinkai) structured? A: A Conciliation Committee consists of one presiding Conciliation Judge (Chōtei Kan-an) and two or more lay Conciliation Commissioners (Chōtei Iin) selected by the Supreme Court of Japan from legal, financial, engineering, corporate, and medical backgrounds.

Q: Why do external non-judge mediators in Indonesia face high roster attrition? A: Public court budgets in Indonesia currently lack dedicated line items to compensate external non-judge mediators. External mediators must rely on voluntary party-paid fees, creating financial hurdles for lower-income litigants and leading to high attrition among certified non-judge professionals.

Q: What are the primary proposals for adapting Japan's model in Indonesian courts? A: Recommended reforms include amending PERMA 1/2016 to establish Tripartite Conciliation Panels, codifying a mandatory 10-day Issue-Sorting Phase, issuing a Joint Ministerial Decree (SKB) for state-funded non-judge mediator compensation, and upgrading PERMA 3/2022 digital mediation infrastructure.

## About This Episode

In this episode, Cecep Mustafa examines Japan's judicial case management architecture under the 2022 Code of Civil Procedure Amendment and the Act on Speeding Up Trials. He analyzes how Japanese courts utilize Court Clerks (Saibansho Shokikan), front-loaded Preparatory Proceedings, and a three-phase digital transformation approach to strengthen docket efficiency, case preparation, and procedural coordination. Cecep Mustafa then compares Japanese practice with Indonesia's SIPP, EIS, and SEMA No. 2 of 2014 framework. The episode presents a structured 30-60-90 day reform blueprint to strengthen pre-trial issue formulation, improve case-flow management, enhance judicial performance measurement, and promote more efficient and predictable court proceedings.

## Listen to the Episode

Optimizing Court Case Management: Japan's Pre-Trial Scheduling and Docket Efficiency

## Key Topics

Japan Case Management, Saibansho Shokikan, Preparatory Proceedings, Act on Speeding Up Trials, Saikō Saibansho Jimusokyoku, SIPP, SEMA 2 2014, Digital Court Transformation.

## Why This Topic Matters

Efficient court case management directly impacts judicial performance, access to justice, and public trust. A well-designed case management architecture ensures that legal disputes transition smoothly from registration to final judgment without unnecessary delays or administrative burdens. Examining Japan's centralized civil case management and front-loaded pre-trial procedures offers practical insights for courts seeking to balance rapid case turnover with thorough, high-quality adjudication.

## Japan Perspective

Japan's civil case management system is governed by the Code of Civil Procedure and the Act on Speeding Up Trials. Intake is managed by Court Clerks (Saibansho Shoki-kan) within Summary Courts (Saimu Saibansho) for claims up to 1.4 million yen, or District Courts (Chihō Saibansho) for claims exceeding 1.4 million yen. Administrative court heads assign cases to single judges or three-judge benches based on statutory complexity, specialized subject matter, and judicial workload distribution algorithms.

Pre-trial procedure relies on front-loaded issue organization known as Preparatory Proceedings. Judges and legal counsel establish structured schedules to narrow disputed issues before formal evidentiary hearings occur. While the Act on Speeding Up Trials establishes a general policy benchmark to resolve first-instance civil cases within 2 years, Japanese District Courts achieve average resolution times between 8 and 12 months. Specialized cases at the Intellectual Property High Court (Chaitai-sai) average between 6.7 and 9.6 months.

Overall litigation volume in Japan remains low relative to population size, with District Courts handling approximately 216,000 total filings annually, including 146,000 civil first-instance suits. Summary Courts handle roughly 1.45 million filings per year. Systemic backlogs are prevented because court-annexed conciliation (Chotei) resolves over 50 percent of civil disputes prior to trial.

Digitalization is governed by the 2022 Code of Civil Procedure Amendment across three statutory phases: Phase 1 establishes web conferencing (primarily Microsoft Teams) for preparatory proceedings; Phase 2 mandates e-filing and digital file management; Phase 3 implements complete e-Court integration and digital records. Performance monitoring is conducted internally by the General Secretariat of the Supreme Court (Saikō Saibansho Jimu-sokyoku), evaluating judges on disposition speed, settlement ratios, appeal reversal rates, and procedural quality.

COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE A comparative analysis between Japan and Indonesia reveals contrasting operational philosophies and organizational models in court case management.

Both jurisdictions utilize digital case management portals and maintain high Supreme Court productivity. Indonesia operates e-Court under PERMA No. 1 of 2019 and PERMA No. 7 of 2022, alongside e-Berpadu under PERMA No. 8 of 2022. In 2024, Indonesia's Supreme Court handled 31,138 total cases, deciding 30,908 cases for a 99.26 percent clearance rate. Japan similarly maintains minimal backlogs, supported by high pre-trial settlement rates through Chotei.

However, key operational differences exist: First, Indonesia enforces a strict 5-month target for first-instance civil trials under Supreme Court Circular Letter (SEMA) No. 2 of 2014. In contrast, Japan relies on the Act on Speeding Up Trials 2-year policy benchmark, achieving 8 to 12 month average civil trial durations through intensive pre-trial issue organization.

Second, Indonesia's digital architecture operates through parallel software platforms: SIPP for case tracking, e-Court for civil filings, e-Berpadu for criminal integration, and EIS (Evaluasi Implementasi SIPP) for performance monitoring. Japan executes a statutory three-phase digital transformation amending the primary Code of Civil Procedure.

Third, performance monitoring in Indonesia relies on automated data compliance scoring through EIS v3, evaluating courts on data entry timeliness. In Japan, the General Secretariat evaluates judicial output, settlement efficacy, and substantive decision stability.

Systemic bottlenecks differ accordingly. Indonesia faces EIS data aggregation challenges, summons service delivery failures under SEMA No. 1 of 2023 registered mail protocols, and e-Berpadu manual fallback occurrences. Japan faces procedural pressure known as mediatory adjudication, where judges heavily evaluated on settlement quotas may exert pressure during conciliation, as well as legacy cultural reliance on physical documentation and name seals (Hanko).

Observe → Understand → Compare → Adapt → Pilot → Improve

The operational methodology for adapting Japanese case management insights into Indonesian court reform follows six structured stages:

Observe: Identify operational friction in Indonesian trial courts, including manual audit overhead in EIS v3, summons delivery delays under SEMA 1/2023, and lack of pre-trial issue narrowing.

Understand: Recognize that Japan's docket efficiency relies on front-loaded Preparatory Proceedings (sōten seiri), Court Clerk intake administration, and judicial evaluation tied to settlement quality rather than raw entry speed.

Compare: Contrast Indonesia's rigid 5-month SEMA 2/2014 deadline against Japan's procedural pre-trial narrowing under the Code of Civil Procedure and Act on Speeding Up Trials.

Adapt: Formulate four targeted technical and administrative reform proposals for Mahkamah Agung:

Technical upgrade to EIS 4.0 featuring granular automated anomaly detection to eliminate manual audit overhead for Supervisory Judges (Hakim Pengawas Bidang).

Integration of an address verification API connecting e-Court with Ministry of Home Affairs (Dukcapil) population records and PT Pos Indonesia logistics tracking to validate postal summonses.

Codification of a mandatory Pre-Trial Issue Formulation Conference (Musyawarah Pra-Sidang) via a new PERMA to narrow contested issues before receiving evidence.

Permanent statutory codification of e-litigation and e-Berpadu workflows into primary procedural codes (RUU KUHAP and RUU Hukum Acara Perdata).

Pilot: Deploy a 90-day pilot program across five representative courts: PN Jakarta Pusat, PN Surakarta, PN Surabaya, PN Makassar, and PN Medan.

Improve: Measure pilot performance against six quantitative Key Performance Indicators:

EIS audit time burden reduced from 8-12 hours per week to under 1.5 hours per week.

Summons delivery accuracy increased from 70-75 percent to over 92 percent.

Average first-instance civil duration reduced from 4.2-4.8 months to under 3.5 months.

e-Berpadu manual paper fallback rate reduced from 15-25 percent to under 3 percent.

Pre-trial issue narrowing rate increased from 0 percent to over 80 percent of pilot cases entering trial with a binding Order on Scope (Penetapan Lingkup Sengketa).

EIS system compliance conversion score sustained above 98.5 percent.

## Judicial Knowledge Takeaways

Front-Loaded Pre-Trial Issue Formulation Speeds Adjudication: Conducting structured pre-trial conferences to narrow legal and factual issues prevents piecemeal hearings and shortens overall trial duration.

Granular Automated Monitoring Reduces Audit Overhead: Upgrading performance platforms to flag specific non-compliant case files automatically removes manual tracking burdens from supervisory judges.

API Integration Fixes Summons Delivery Vulnerabilities: Connecting court filing portals directly with population registries and postal logistics services ensures accurate service and reduces default judgments.

Primary Legislative Codification Secures Digital Litigation: Embedding electronic court procedures into primary national procedural codes eliminates procedural challenges regarding online witness testimony and digital records.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is the statutory time benchmark for civil trials in Japan? A: The Act on Speeding Up Trials sets a general policy benchmark to dispose of first-instance civil cases within 2 years, though Japanese District Courts achieve average resolution times between 8 and 12 months.

Q: How does Japan manage case intake and judicial assignment? A: Court Clerks (Saibansho Shoki-kan) manage intake in Summary Courts for claims up to 1.4 million yen and District Courts for larger claims. Administrative court heads assign cases to single judges or three-judge benches based on complexity and workload algorithms.

Q: How does Indonesia evaluate local court case management performance? A: Indonesia utilizes Evaluasi Implementasi SIPP (EIS), an automated software platform managed by Ditjen Badilum that scores local courts on data entry compliance, document completeness, and operational timeliness.

Q: What are the main features of Japan's civil digital court transformation? A: Enacted under the 2022 Code of Civil Procedure Amendment, Japan's digital transformation follows three phases: Phase 1 web conferencing for preparatory hearings, Phase 2 mandatory e-filing and digitized records, and Phase 3 full online e-Court litigation.

Q: What is the proposed Pre-Trial Issue Formulation Conference for Indonesian courts? A: It is a proposed mandatory pre-trial conference (Musyawarah Pra-Sidang) where parties present documentary evidence and arguments early, allowing judges to issue a binding Order on Scope of Trial (Penetapan Lingkup Sengketa) that limits subsequent oral hearings.

## About This Episode

In this episode, Cecep Mustafa examines Japan's centralized public legal aid framework through the Japan Legal Support Center (Hōterasu), established under the Comprehensive Legal Support Act of 2004. He analyzes how Japan deploys salaried staff attorneys (jōkin bengoshi) to underserved and depopulated rural areas (kasochi shusshōjo) to expand access to legal assistance and address geographic barriers to justice. Cecep Mustafa then compares the Hōterasu model with Indonesia's legal aid architecture under Law No. 16 of 2011 and Supreme Court Regulation (PERMA) No. 1 of 2014. The episode presents a practical blueprint for establishing Public Defender Stations (Sentra Advokat Publik) in frontier court jurisdictions, focusing on geographic access, institutional coordination, sustainable legal assistance, and equal access to justice.

## Listen to the Episode

Securing Universal Access to Justice: Japan's Hōterasu Model for Public Legal Aid Reform

## Key Topics

Japan Legal Aid, Hōterasu, Comprehensive Legal Support Act, Salaried Staff Attorneys, Kasochi Outposts, BPHN Legal Aid, Posbakum, Sentra Advokat Publik.

## Why This Topic Matters

Access to legal representation is a fundamental requirement for realizing the rule of law. When indigent or geographically isolated citizens cannot access affordable counsel, statutory rights fail to produce substantive remedies. In decentralized or archipelagic nations, relying solely on private law firms or non-governmental organizations creates severe regional legal aid deficits. Examining Japan's centralized public legal aid corporation provides actionable strategies for structuring public defender networks, managing legal assistance funds, and delivering equitable legal aid in underserved regions.

## Japan Perspective

Japan's public legal aid framework is governed by the Comprehensive Legal Support Act of 2004. In 2006, the Ministry of Justice established the Japan Legal Support Center, widely known as Hōterasu, as a specialized public corporation. Supported by a central annual budget of approximately JPY 32.1 billion, Hōterasu operates a nationwide network designed to prevent legal aid coverage gaps.

Hōterasu provides three free 30-minute consultations per legal issue for low-income citizens. For formal litigation, it administers a civil legal aid loan system (minji hōritsu fujo) that advances attorney retainer fees (chakushukin) and procedural expenses. Beneficiaries repay these interest-free advances in monthly installments ranging from JPY 5,000 to JPY 10,000, with full repayment waivers available for prolonged financial hardship.

To overcome market-driven legal aid deficits in rural areas, Hōterasu directly employs salaried staff attorneys (jōkin bengoshi). These public advocates are deployed across 50 regional main branches and dedicated remote outposts (kasochi shusshōjo). Eligibility is determined through a unified financial intake algorithm that evaluates gross income alongside mandatory household expenditure allowances, enabling near-poor citizens to receive structured fee advancements rather than facing total exclusion. Hōterasu also operates a Multilingual Information Service in ten languages to assist foreign residents and language minorities.

COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE A comparative assessment highlights fundamental structural differences between the legal aid models of Japan and Indonesia.

In Indonesia, state-funded legal aid is governed by Law No. 16 of 2011 on Legal Aid, administered by the National Legal Development Agency (BPHN) under the Ministry of Law and Human Rights. For the 2025 to 2027 verification cycle, BPHN certified 597 accredited Legal Aid Organizations (OBH), categorized into Tiers A, B, and C based on personnel and litigation volume. Concurrently, first-instance courts operate Court Legal Aid Posts (Posbakum) under Perma No. 1 of 2014, funded via judicial budget allocations (DIPA MA) to provide preliminary document drafting and consultation.

However, the two systems diverge in operational delivery and coverage consistency:

First, Indonesia relies on external non-governmental OBHs that receive fixed lump-sum reimbursements per completed litigation phase. Because fixed reimbursements often do not cover actual travel and operational costs in remote island or mountainous regions, private legal aid organizations incur net losses when taking complex civil or land disputes in outer territories. This results in a severe legal aid deficit outside major urban centers in Java and Bali, leaving indigent civil representation rates below 10 percent in many rural courts.

Second, Indonesia's system separates courthouse advice desks (Posbakum) from external litigation defense (OBH). In contrast, Japan's Hōterasu internalizes service delivery through a single statutory corporation that deploys full-time salaried advocates directly to underserved areas (kasochi), decoupling legal assistance from local private market viability.

Observe → Understand → Compare → Adapt → Pilot → Improve

The operational methodology for adapting Japan's public legal aid insights into Indonesian court reform follows six structured steps:

Observe: Identify geographic coverage gaps and financial losses faced by accredited legal aid organizations attempting to serve rural litigants under Indonesia's lump-sum reimbursement system.

Understand: Recognize that Hōterasu maintains universal coverage by employing salaried staff attorneys (jōkin bengoshi) and deploying them directly to depopulated areas (kasochi) using centralized budget allocations.

Compare: Contrast Indonesia's fragmented non-governmental grant model against Japan's centralized public legal corporation architecture.

Adapt: Formulate specific regulatory and institutional proposals for Indonesia:

Promulgate a Joint Decree (SKB Tiga Lembaga) between the Ministry of Law and Human Rights, Ministry of Finance, and Supreme Court to create a National Public Defender Roster and Civil Litigation Advancement Scheme (Skema Talangan Biaya Perkara).

Establish permanent Public Defender Stations (Sentra Advokat Publik) inside Class II District and Religious Courts in frontier, outermost, and underdeveloped regions (Wilayah 3T), staffed by salaried Public Advocates (Advokat Publik Kontrak).

Automate indigence verification by linking court e-Court and Posbakum portals directly to the Ministry of Social Affairs Unified Social Welfare Registry (DTKS) for instant fee waivers (prodeo).

Pilot: Deploy a 90-day pilot program placing two full-time accredited Public Advocates and an autonomous revolving fee advancement fund in three isolated jurisdictions: PN/PA Wamena (Papua Pegunungan), Saumlaki (Maluku), and Tahuna (Sulawesi Utara).

Improve: Evaluate pilot outcomes against established benchmarks, targeting an increase in indigent civil representation from under 10 percent to at least 45 percent, and reducing prodeo verification processing times from 14 business days to under 24 hours.

## Judicial Knowledge Takeaways

Salaried Public Advocates Eliminate Geographic Coverage Gaps: Deploying full-time salaried staff attorneys to depopulated regions ensures continuous legal aid coverage that does not depend on local private market profitability.

Flexible Fee Advancement Assists the Near-Poor: Implementing interest-free fee advancement loans with sliding scale repayments prevents near-poor litigants from being excluded by rigid income cutoffs.

Automated Social Registry Integration Speeds Fee Waivers: Connecting court intake portals directly to national social welfare databases eliminates multi-tiered paper certification delays for indigent litigants.

Coordinated Inter-Agency Governance Secures Stable Budgeting: Establishing joint decree frameworks across judicial, legal, and financial ministries secures multi-year operational budgets for rural public legal defender outposts.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is the statutory basis and budget of Japan's Hōterasu? A: Hōterasu was established under the Comprehensive Legal Support Act of 2004 and launched in 2006 under the Ministry of Justice, operating with a central annual budget of approximately JPY 32.1 billion.

Q: How does Hōterasu serve depopulated rural areas in Japan? A: Hōterasu directly hires salaried staff attorneys (jōkin bengoshi) and stations them across 50 regional main branches and dedicated depopulated rural outposts (kasochi shusshōjo).

Q: How is state-funded legal aid currently structured in Indonesia? A: Indonesian legal aid is governed by Law No. 16 of 2011, under which BPHN accredits 597 non-governmental Legal Aid Organizations (OBH) that receive fixed lump-sum reimbursements per litigation stage, alongside court-funded Posbakum consultation desks under Perma No. 1 of 2014.

Q: What is the proposed Sentra Advokat Publik model for Indonesian courts? A: The proposal establishes permanent Public Defender Stations embedded inside Class II courts in frontier regions (Wilayah 3T), staffed by salaried Public Advocates (Advokat Publik Kontrak) and supported by an automated DTKS social welfare verification gateway.

Q: What are the performance targets for the 90-day legal aid pilot in Wamena, Saumlaki, and Tahuna? A: The pilot targets increasing indigent civil legal representation from under 10 percent to at least 45 percent and reducing civil fee-waiver (prodeo) verification times from 14 business days to under 24 hours.

## About This Episode

In this episode, Cecep Mustafa examines Japan's judicial education architecture centered at the Legal Training and Research Institute (Shihō Kenshūjo) under the Supreme Court of Japan. He analyzes how structured clinical apprenticeships, co-mediation simulation modules, and periodic jurisprudence seminars can develop neutral facilitation competencies, practical courtroom skills, and reflective judicial practice. Cecep Mustafa then compares Japan's judicial training approach with Indonesia's mediator certification framework under Supreme Court Regulation (PERMA) No. 1 of 2016 and SK KMA No. 117/KMA/SKA/IV/2018. The episode presents a practical blueprint for clinical judicial education reform at BSDK Kumdil, emphasizing experiential learning, simulation-based training, continuous professional development, standardized competencies, and evidence-based evaluation of judicial mediation practice.

## Listen to the Episode

Professionalizing Judicial Personnel: Japan's Legal Training Institute and Clinical Competency Frameworks

## Key Topics

Shiho Kenshujo, Judicial Education, Clinical Apprenticeship, Co Mediation Dynamics, BSDK Kumdil, Mediator Certification, PERMA 1 2016, Judicial Competency.

## Why This Topic Matters

The quality of judicial dispute resolution depends directly on the professional competence and ethical standards of judicial personnel. While procedural regulations establish formal frameworks for court-annexed mediation, facilitation skills cannot be acquired solely through lecture-based instruction in statutory norms. Examining how Japan structures clinical judicial education provides valuable strategies for moving beyond basic 40-hour administrative certification courses toward continuous, simulation-driven judicial development.

## Japan Perspective

Judicial education in Japan is centralized under the Supreme Court of Japan at the Legal Training and Research Institute (Shihō Kenshūjo). The institute oversees induction training for legal apprentices (shūshūsei) who have passed the National Bar Examination, as well as continuing professional education for appointed career judges (saibankan).

The curriculum at Shihō Kenshūjo combines theoretical analysis of civil procedure with practical clinical apprenticeships in courtrooms. For civil conciliation (Minji Chōtei), training emphasizes interest-based negotiation, psychological de-escalation, and preliminary evidentiary analysis (sōten seiri). Career judges designated as Conciliation Judges (Chōtei-kan) receive specialized instruction in supervising lay Conciliation Commissioners (Chōtei-iin) and managing multi-member panel dynamics.

Continuing education is maintained through structured seminars organized by High Courts and the National Conciliation Association Federation (Nihon Chōtei Kyōkai Rengōkai). These programs utilize casebooks (Chōteiin Hikkei), mock conciliation sessions (mock conciliation), and peer record audits to ensure uniform facilitation standards across all judicial districts.

COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE A comparative assessment reveals significant differences in judicial education structures between Japan and Indonesia.

In Indonesia, judicial education and mediator certification are managed by the Judicial Policy Strategy and Training Body (BSDK Kumdil) through its Technical Judicial Training Center (Pusdiklat Teknis Peradilan). Active career judges complete certified mediation courses conducted by BSDK. For non-judge mediators, certification is provided by university centers and private training institutes accredited under SK KMA No. 117/KMA/SKA/IV/2018, requiring a minimum 40-classroom-hour curriculum.

Key operational differences include:

First, Indonesia's 40-hour certification course focuses primarily on normative legal lectures and basic role-play exercises. The system lacks mandatory clinical courtroom apprenticeships or post-certification supervised practice prior to court roster placement.

Second, Indonesia maintains no statutory requirement for periodic re-certification or performance-based portfolio audits for accredited non-judge mediators. Once certified, mediators remain on court rosters without systematic quality oversight.

Third, training for judge mediators does not cover co-mediation dynamics (co-mediation dynamic) with external technical experts, leaving career judges unprepared to lead hybrid panels.

In contrast, Japan's Shihō Kenshūjo embeds multi-month clinical apprenticeships into core legal training and maintains continuous professional development through regional judicial associations.

Observe → Understand → Compare → Adapt → Pilot → Improve

The operational methodology for adapting Japanese judicial training insights into Indonesian court reform follows six structured stages:

Observe: Identify skill deficits in Indonesian court mediation, where 40-hour lecture courses leave mediators underprepared for complex commercial or land disputes.

Understand: Recognize that Japanese conciliation quality is sustained through Shihō Kenshūjo clinical apprenticeships, standardized casebooks, and continuous peer review.

Compare: Contrast Indonesia's static 40-hour certification model against Japan's integrated clinical training and lifelong judicial education framework.

Adapt: Formulate specific training reform proposals under the JPAIS-MED-TRN-001 framework for BSDK Kumdil:

Restructure the 40-hour certification curriculum to include 20 hours of clinical case simulations based on actual court dossiers.

Mandate a 30-day clinical court apprenticeship (pemagangan klinis) at first-instance courts before roster placement.

Introduce a specialized curriculum on co-mediation dynamics for judge mediators and external expert commissioners.

Enact a mandatory 3-year re-certification requirement (mandatory re-certification) evaluated through settlement portfolio audits.

Pilot: Launch the revised clinical training module at BSDK Kumdil for 60 judge mediators and 30 external expert candidates serving pilot courts.

Improve: Evaluate training efficacy against participant procedural justice satisfaction scores (target PJSS >= 4.30 out of 5.00) and initial pilot court settlement conversion rates.

## Judicial Knowledge Takeaways

Clinical Apprenticeships Build Practical Facilitation Skills: Courtroom apprenticeships under experienced mentors prepare trainees for complex dispute dynamics far more effectively than classroom lectures.

Co-Mediation Training Enables Hybrid Panel Success: Instructing judges and technical experts in joint panel facilitation resolves role ambiguity and improves negotiation leadership.

Mandatory Re-Certification Sustains Professional Standards: Requiring periodic re-certification based on portfolio audits removes inactive or underperforming neutrals from official court rosters.

Standardized Benchbooks Ensure National Consistency: Publishing detailed operational handbooks maintains uniform ethical and procedural standards across regional court jurisdictions.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What institution manages judicial education in Japan? A: Judicial education in Japan is centralized at the Legal Training and Research Institute (Shihō Kenshūjo), an organ of the Supreme Court of Japan.

Q: How is non-judge mediator certification structured in Indonesia? A: Non-judge mediator certification in Indonesia requires a minimum 40-hour course delivered by training organizations accredited by the Supreme Court under SK KMA No. 117/KMA/SKA/IV/2018.

Q: What is the main limitation of Indonesia's current mediator training model? A: The current model relies heavily on theoretical lectures without requiring clinical courtroom apprenticeships, supervised practice, or periodic re-certification.

Q: What is the JPAIS-MED-TRN-001 training proposal? A: JPAIS-MED-TRN-001 is a proposed BSDK Kumdil curriculum reform introducing 20 hours of clinical case simulations, a 30-day court apprenticeship, co-mediation instruction, and a 3-year re-certification requirement.

Q: How does Japan maintain quality control among lay conciliation commissioners? A: Japan maintains quality control through regional High Court seminars, the National Conciliation Association Federation, standardized handbooks (Chōteiin Hikkei), and regular peer reviews.

## About This Episode

In this episode, Cecep Mustafa examines Japan's civil court digitalization under the Code of Civil Procedure Amendments (Act No. 48 of 2022) and the 2023 Integration Act (Act No. 53 of 2023), with particular attention to the mints platform and the use of web conferencing in court-annexed conciliation. He compares Japan's digital judicial infrastructure with Indonesia's Electronic Court Mediation framework under Supreme Court Regulation (PERMA) No. 3 of 2022, exploring how digital platforms can support more accessible, efficient, and secure dispute resolution. Cecep Mustafa then outlines technical and procedural enhancements for Indonesian trial courts, focusing on modernizing virtual caucuses, strengthening digital evidence management, and improving electronic signature validation. The episode highlights how interoperable digital infrastructure and clear procedural safeguards can support the next generation of technology-enabled court mediation.

## Listen to the Episode

Digitizing Court Mediation: Japan's Civil IT Transformation and E-Mediation Frameworks

## Key Topics

Digital Mediation, mints Platform, PERMA 3 2022, Act 48 2022, E-Court Indonesia, Electronic Signature, Virtual Caucus, Soten Seiri.

## Why This Topic Matters

Integrating digital technology into court-annexed mediation reduces geographic travel barriers, lowers dispute resolution costs, and speeds up document exchange. However, digitalizing dispute resolution without structured pre-trial preparation can create technical hurdles and reduce interpersonal engagement, particularly in complex commercial or sensitive family cases. Analyzing Japan's statutory civil court digitalization offers actionable technical and procedural insights for enhancing electronic mediation while safeguarding due process and procedural fairness.

## Japan Perspective

Japan's civil litigation digitalization is established under amendments to the Code of Civil Procedure (Act No. 48 of 2022) and the 2023 Integration Act (Act No. 53 of 2023). The statutory reform establishes a full digital transition structured across three technological pillars.

The first pillar is mandatory e-filing. All licensed attorneys are required to submit pleadings, petitions, and documentary evidence electronically through the Supreme Court mints platform.

The second pillar is e-case management, providing judges, legal counsel, and conciliation committees with secure digital access to digitized case records.

The third pillar is e-court proceedings, incorporating web-conferencing software (primarily Microsoft Teams) for preparatory proceedings, witness examinations, and conciliation hearings.

Digitalization directly supports Japan's civil conciliation infrastructure (Minji Chōtei). By requiring advance digital submission of pleadings and documentary evidence, Conciliation Committees (Chōtei Iinkai) conduct pre-session issue-sorting (sōten seiri). This enables panels to assess complex financial and property disputes efficiently, keeping virtual sessions focused on core valuation issues. Over the past decade, self-represented (pro se) litigation in Japanese district courts decreased from 20 percent to 7 percent as representation standardized around digital workflows.

COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE A comparative evaluation reveals contrasting technological architectures and operational realities between Japan and Indonesia.

Both legal systems have promulgated statutory rules to authorize online court proceedings. Indonesia enacted Supreme Court Regulation (PERMA) No. 3 of 2022 to govern Electronic Court Mediation (Mediasi di Pengadilan Secara Elektronik) within its existing e-Court portal. PERMA 3/2022 permits virtual teleconferencing upon party consent or mediator determination and authorizes electronic signatures (tanda tangan elektronik) for mediation schedules, caucus notes, and final Settlement Deeds (Akta Dading). Japan enacted Act No. 48 of 2022 to mandate digital filing via mints and authorize web-conferencing for conciliation and trial hearings.

However, operational implementation reflects key structural differences.

In Indonesia, e-mediation under PERMA 3/2022 effectively reduces travel expenses for urban and corporate litigants. However, its adoption in regional courts remains constrained by internet bandwidth disparities and a lack of dedicated virtual caucus software. Furthermore, online sessions in sensitive family disputes can limit a mediator's ability to evaluate non-verbal cues.

In Japan, digital conciliation is integrated directly into structured issue-sorting (sōten seiri). Digitized evidence is reviewed by the panel prior to online hearings, ensuring that virtual sessions address specific financial or legal impasses rather than unstructured discussions.

Observe → Understand → Compare → Adapt → Pilot → Improve

The operational methodology for adapting Japanese e-litigation practices into Indonesian court reform follows six structured stages:

Observe: Identify operational constraints in Indonesia's e-mediation under PERMA 3/2022, including internet connectivity gaps in regional courts and unintegrated virtual caucus tools.

Understand: Recognize that Japan's digital conciliation succeeds because online hearings are paired with advance digital document submission and structured issue-sorting (sōten seiri).

Compare: Contrast Indonesia's voluntary e-mediation portal against Japan's mandatory e-filing system (mints) and web-conferencing architecture under Act No. 48 of 2022.

Adapt: Formulate four technical and procedural upgrades for Mahkamah Agung under PERMA 3/2022:

Build secure digital evidence rooms (Ruang Bukti Digital) within the e-Court portal for advance document uploads prior to mediation sessions.

Integrate automated scheduling and virtual caucus breakout rooms into the e-mediation software interface.

Embed certified electronic signature validation (tanda tangan elektronik tersertifikasi) for remote signing of Settlement Deeds (Akta Dading).

Establish bandwidth allocation standards and hardware specifications for trial court virtual mediation rooms.

Pilot: Deploy the upgraded e-mediation module across four pilot courts: PN Jakarta Selatan, PA Jakarta Selatan, PN Surabaya, and PA Sleman.

Improve: Measure performance against target pilot benchmarks, aiming for at least 30 percent of pilot mediation sessions conducted online, 100 percent digital signature compliance, and a reduction in average settlement duration to 18 calendar days or fewer.

## Judicial Knowledge Takeaways

Pre-Session Document Digitization Sharpens Virtual Hearings: Requiring advance digital submission of evidence allows neutrals to review facts beforehand and conduct focused online sessions.

Integrated Virtual Caucuses Preserve Negotiation Confidentiality: Embedding secure breakout rooms into court platforms enables mediators to conduct private caucuses without leaving the primary virtual session.

Certified Electronic Signatures Ensure Settlement Validity: Incorporating verified digital signatures prevents post-settlement challenges regarding party authorization and consent.

Technical Infrastructure Must Match Procedural Mandates: Deploying online mediation rules requires standardized courtroom hardware and internet bandwidth guarantees to prevent procedural delays.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What statutes govern civil court digitalization in Japan? A: Civil court digitalization in Japan is governed by amendments to the Code of Civil Procedure (Act No. 48 of 2022) and the 2023 Integration Act (Act No. 53 of 2023).

Q: What is Japan's mints platform? A: The mints platform is the official Supreme Court of Japan digital system used by licensed attorneys for mandatory electronic filing of pleadings and documentary evidence.

Q: What regulation governs electronic court mediation in Indonesia? A: Electronic court mediation in Indonesia is governed by Supreme Court Regulation (PERMA) No. 3 of 2022 on Electronic Court Mediation.

Q: How does advance digital filing improve virtual mediation? A: Advance digital filing allows conciliation committees and mediators to complete early issue-sorting (sōten seiri), ensuring virtual sessions focus on specific legal or financial disagreements.

Q: What technical upgrades are proposed for Indonesia's e-mediation portal? A: Proposed upgrades include secure digital evidence rooms, integrated virtual caucus breakout tools, automated session scheduling, and certified electronic signature validation.

## About This Episode

In this episode, Cecep Mustafa analyzes Japan's civil preparatory proceedings (kōzō chōsei tetsuzuki) under the Code of Civil Procedure (Act No. 109 of 1996) and evaluates their strategic value for civil procedural reform in Indonesia. He examines how Japanese courts use the statutory Right of Clarification (shakumeiken), binding Trial Plans (shinkō keikaku), and inter-party inquiries to identify disputed issues, organize evidence, and improve procedural efficiency before trial. Cecep Mustafa then compares Japanese practice with Indonesia's HIR/RBg framework and PTUN administrative procedures, highlighting opportunities to strengthen pre-trial case preparation. The episode presents a structured reform blueprint for introducing mandatory Civil Preparatory Examinations (Pemeriksaan Persiapan Perdata) in Indonesian District Courts, with a focus on issue identification, evidence management, procedural clarity, judicial case management, and more efficient trials.

## Listen to the Episode

Mastering Civil Preparatory Proceedings: Japan's Pre-Trial Issue Clarification Framework

## Key Topics

Japan Civil Procedure, Preparatory Proceedings, Shakumeiken, Shinkou Keikaku, Pre-Trial Discovery, Obscuur Libel, PTUN Administrative Procedure, E-Litigasi Indonesia.

## Why This Topic Matters

The efficiency of civil adjudication depends largely on how effectively courts and litigants structure legal claims and evidence during the pre-trial phase. Without mandatory pre-trial issue clarification, civil lawsuits often enter trial with vague pleadings, surprise evidence submissions, and unfocused witness hearings. This results in repeated schedule postponements, prolonged litigation, and low settlement rates. Examining Japan's front-loaded pre-trial framework provides actionable insights for shifting civil litigation from passive administrative processing to active judicial management.

## Japan Perspective

Civil litigation in Japan is governed by the Code of Civil Procedure (Act No. 109 of 1996). The 1996 Code reform structurally integrated issue and evidence arrangement proceedings (kozo chosei tetuzuki) into ordinary civil procedure through three statutory options: Preliminary Oral Arguments under Articles 164 through 167, Preparatory Proceedings under Articles 168 through 174, and Written Preparatory Proceedings under Articles 175 through 178.

Active judicial management is grounded in the Presiding Judge's statutory Right of Clarification (shakumeiken) under Article 149. This authority empowers courts to question litigants, require pleading revisions, and order the production of documentary evidence under Article 151. Courts also establish binding Trial Plans (shinkou keikaku) under Article 147-2 to set fixed schedules for issue organization and witness testimony.

To gather necessary facts early, litigants utilize Pre-Filing Inquiries under Article 132-2, Pre-Filing Evidence Collection under Article 132-4, and Inter-Party Inquiries under Article 163. Once preparatory proceedings conclude, Articles 157, 167, 174, and 178 enforce strict preclusion rules, dismissing late allegations or evidence submitted without reasonable justification. Under the Act on Promotion of Speedier Trials (Act No. 107 of 2003), Japanese first-instance proceedings target completion within two years, achieving an actual average trial duration of 9 to 14 months. Furthermore, integrated in-court settlement discussions (Wakai) under Article 89 yield settlement rates between 36 percent and 37.1 percent.

COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE A comparative analysis reveals fundamental structural differences between civil procedure in Japan and Indonesia.

In Indonesia, standard civil litigation in District Courts (Pengadilan Negeri) is governed by legacy colonial codes: the Revised Inlandsch Reglement (HIR) and the Reglement tot Regeling van het Rechtswezen in de Buitengewesten (RBg). The HIR/RBg framework lacks a general, mandatory pre-trial issue clarification stage. Civil suits proceed directly from initial appearances to court-annexed mediation under PERMA No. 1 of 2016, followed immediately by serial written exchanges (jawaban, replik, duplik) and piecemeal evidence presentation in open court.

However, specific statutory sub-jurisdictions in Indonesia demonstrate the viability of active pre-trial management. Administrative Courts (Pengadilan Tata Usaha Negara / PTUN) under Article 63 of Law No. 5 of 1986 mandate a Preparatory Examination (Pemeriksaan Persiapan), granting judges ex-officio authority to order pleading revisions within 30 days and compel administrative document production. Similarly, Small Claims Courts (Gugatan Sederhana) under PERMA No. 2 of 2015 and PERMA No. 4 of 2019 utilize a Preliminary Examination (Pemeriksaan Pendahuluan) by a single judge to verify claim eligibility for monetary claims under Rp 500,000,000. Additionally, PERMA No. 7 of 2022 provides an electronic framework (E-Court and E-Litigasi) for digital document transmission, though it lacks interactive pre-trial issue framing features.

These structural disparities generate contrasting operational metrics. In Indonesian general civil courts, the absence of early issue clarification leads to high rates of interlocutory exceptions for vague pleadings (obscuur libel, occurring in 64.5 percent of cases) and prolonged trial durations averaging 7.5 months despite the 5-month administrative target under SEMA No. 2 of 2014. Mediation success in general civil cases remains low, ranging between 1.4 percent and 5 percent, because parties negotiate before evidence is organized. In Japan, front-loading case preparation yields predictable 9 to 14 month disposition timelines and in-court settlement rates exceeding 36 percent.

Observe → Understand → Compare → Adapt → Pilot → Improve

The methodology for adapting Japanese pre-trial practices into Indonesian civil procedure follows six structured steps:

Observe: Identify systemic trial delays in Indonesian District Courts caused by vague pleadings (obscuur libel), surprise evidence submissions, and passive pre-trial judicial involvement.

Understand: Recognize that Japan achieves civil trial efficiency through statutory issue arrangement proceedings, the Right of Clarification (shakumeiken), and binding procedural preclusion.

Compare: Contrast Indonesia's passive HIR/RBg pre-trial structure with Japan's active issue arrangement under Code of Civil Procedure Articles 164 through 178, while noting existing Indonesian precedents in PTUN Law Article 63 and PERMA No. 4 of 2019.

Adapt: Formulate specific regulatory proposals for Mahkamah Agung under a new Supreme Court Regulation (PERMA) on Civil Preparatory Proceedings (Pemeriksaan Persiapan Perdata / PPP):

Codify judicial ex-officio clarification powers (Hak Menjelaskan) to order pleading rectifications and issue binding Pre-Trial Issue Summaries (Risalah Sengketa) within 14 days.

Establish a Pre-Trial Digital Evidence Disclosure Protocol (PT-DEDP) within E-Court, requiring advance document exchange and joint issue matrices prior to scheduling witness hearings.

Implement a Dual-Track Settlement Mechanism allowing trial judges to conduct Judicial Settlement Conferences post-issue clarification, leveraging factual summaries to guide discussions.

Enforce statutory preclusion rules that forfeit a party's right to introduce late claims or evidence after the preparatory phase closes.

Pilot: Deploy a 90-day pilot program across five Class IA Special District Courts: Central Jakarta, Surabaya, Medan, Bandung, and Makassar.

Improve: Measure pilot performance against clear quantitative benchmarks:

Reduce average first-instance trial duration from 7.5 months to under 4.5 months.

Increase SEMA No. 2 of 2014 5-month target compliance from 58.2 percent to over 92.0 percent.

Raise commercial in-court settlement success rates from 4.1 percent to over 25.0 percent.

Reduce interlocutory exceptions for vague pleadings (obscuur libel) from 64.5 percent to under 15.0 percent of cases.

Decrease average evidentiary trial sessions from 11.4 sessions to under 5.0 sessions per case.

## Judicial Knowledge Takeaways

Active Judicial Clarification Prevents Trial Detours: Empowering judges to question litigants and order pleading rectifications early eliminates vague claims (obscuur libel) before trial.

Pre-Trial Evidence Disclosure Eliminates Surprise Submissions: Requiring mutual document exchange prior to witness hearings prevents unexpected postponements and focuses oral testimony.

Binding Procedural Calendars Enforce Trial Discipline: Establishing fixed schedules with strict preclusion rules for late evidence ensures compliance with statutory disposition targets.

Post-Clarification Settlement Increases Resolution Rates: Facilitating settlement discussions after issues and evidence are clarified provides litigants with a realistic basis for compromise.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is the Presiding Judge's Right of Clarification (shakumeiken) in Japan? A: Grounded in Article 149 of the Japanese Code of Civil Procedure, the Right of Clarification authorizes the presiding judge to ask questions, request pleading revisions, and order parties to produce evidence on or outside scheduled hearing dates.

Q: Does Indonesian law contain any existing examples of pre-trial preparatory examinations? A: Yes. Article 63 of Law No. 5 of 1986 governing Administrative Courts (PTUN) mandates a Preparatory Examination (Pemeriksaan Persiapan), and PERMA No. 4 of 2019 governing Small Claims Courts includes a single-judge Preliminary Examination (Pemeriksaan Pendahuluan).

Q: What is the proposed Civil Preparatory Examination (Pemeriksaan Persiapan Perdata) for Indonesian District Courts? A: It is a proposed mandatory pre-trial phase conducted by judges in District Courts to review pleadings, enforce digital evidence disclosure, issue binding Pre-Trial Issue Summaries (Risalah Sengketa), and conduct post-clarification settlement conferences.

Q: How does Japan handle evidence submitted late in civil proceedings? A: Under Articles 157, 157-2, 167, 174, and 178 of the Japanese Code of Civil Procedure, courts have statutory authority to dismiss allegations or evidence submitted late due to intent or gross negligence after preparatory proceedings close.

Q: What performance targets are set for the 90-day Civil Preparatory Examination pilot in Indonesia? A: Targets include reducing average trial duration to under 4.5 months, increasing SEMA 2/2014 timeline compliance above 92 percent, raising commercial settlement rates above 25 percent, and reducing vague pleading exceptions below 15 percent.

## About This Episode

In this episode, Cecep Mustafa examines Japan's court-annexed civil conciliation (Chōtei) framework under the Civil Conciliation Act (Act No. 222 of 1951) and the Domestic Relations Case Procedure Act (Act No. 52 of 2011). He explores how Japan utilizes multidisciplinary Conciliation Committees (Chōtei Iinkai) and judicial Orders in Lieu of Conciliation (Chōtei ni kawaru kettei) under Article 17 to facilitate negotiated settlements in civil and family disputes. The episode considers reported settlement outcomes in general civil and complex inheritance matters while examining the institutional mechanisms that support effective court-connected conciliation. Cecep Mustafa then contrasts the Japanese framework with Indonesia's PERMA No. 1 of 2016 and presents a structured 90-day pilot model for Indonesian trial courts. The proposed model introduces Tripartite Conciliation Panels (Majelis Konsiliasi Tripartit) and Orders in Lieu of Settlement (Penetapan Pengganti Perdamaian), with a focus on multidisciplinary dispute resolution, judicial oversight, settlement quality, procedural efficiency, and access to justice.

## Listen to the Episode

Transforming Court Mediation: Japan's Chōtei Model and Orders in Lieu of Settlement

## Key Topics

Japan Civil Conciliation, Minji Chōtei Hō, Chōtei Iinkai, Order in Lieu of Conciliation, Chōtei Zenchi Shugi, PERMA 1 2016, Majelis Konsiliasi Tripartit, Penetapan Pengganti Perdamaian.

## Why This Topic Matters

Court-connected mediation is vital for alleviating trial docket congestion and promoting consensual dispute resolution. However, when mediation operates under a solo-mediator model lacking domain expertise or evaluative authority, proceedings often degenerate into formalistic administrative hurdles. In Indonesian general civil courts (Pengadilan Negeri), mediation success rates hover between 4.0 percent and 4.08 percent. Analyzing Japan's hybrid conciliation architecture offers actionable insights for equipping court neutrals with evaluative settlement tools and multi-disciplinary expert panels.

## Japan Perspective

Japan's civil conciliation system is governed by the Civil Conciliation Act (Minji Chōtei Hō, Act No. 222 of 1951) and the Domestic Relations Case Procedure Act (Kaji Jiken Tetsuzuki Hō, Act No. 52 of 2011). Rather than relying on isolated judicial officers, conciliation is conducted by a Tripartite Conciliation Committee (Chōtei Iinkai) comprising one career judge (the Chief Conciliator) and two lay Civil Conciliation Commissioners (Minji Chōtei-in). These commissioners are appointed by the Supreme Court of Japan from professional backgrounds, including attorneys, certified public accountants, real estate appraisers, architects, and experienced community leaders.

Under Article 257 of the Domestic Relations Case Procedure Act and Article 24-2 of the Civil Conciliation Act, Japan enforces Chōtei Zenchi Shugi, requiring mandatory conciliation prior to litigation in domestic relations, inheritance, and real estate rent disputes.

When negotiating parties reach a narrow impasse, Article 17 of the Civil Conciliation Act empowers the court to issue an Order in Lieu of Conciliation (Chōtei ni kawaru kettei) ex officio. After consulting the committee, the court crafts an equitable resolution balancing the parties' rights. Unless a party files an objection within a statutory two-week window, the order gains the identical legal force of a final court judgment. In domestic relations matters, an equivalent decree (Kaji Shimbai ni kawaru kettei) under Article 284 yields a 71.8 percent aggregate resolution rate in complex inheritance divisions (isan bunkatsu), combining 42.0 percent direct agreements with 29.9 percent un-objected judicial orders. Non-appearance is deterred by administrative fines up to 50,000 yen under Article 349.

## Comparative Perspective

Comparing court-connected dispute resolution between Japan and Indonesia reveals critical structural differences.

In Indonesia, court mediation is governed by Supreme Court Regulation (PERMA) No. 1 of 2016. The system relies on a solo mediator model, assigning either a single career judge mediator or a solo non-judge mediator. General civil courts (Pengadilan Negeri) record national mediation success rates between 4.0 percent and 4.08 percent. While religious courts (Pengadilan Agama) report a higher composite success rate of 39.85 percent, this figure is largely driven by uncontested divorce petition withdrawals; contentious commercial and Islamic banking claims in religious courts yield settlement rates below 15 percent. Furthermore, non-judge mediator success in courts like Tangerang Religious Court drops to 7.04 percent due to uncompensated pro-bono status and lack of state budget allowances.

Indonesian mediators lack evaluative authority to issue proposed settlement orders when parties reach a narrow deadlock. Additionally, trial judges rarely enforce procedural cost sanctions for bad-faith non-appearance under Article 7 of PERMA 1/2016, allowing dilatory tactics.

In contrast, Japan's model combines judicial authority with lay expert knowledge, providing evaluative orders that bridge negotiation gaps while maintaining strict statutory penalties for non-attendance.

Observe → Understand → Compare → Adapt → Pilot → Improve

The pathway for adapting Japanese conciliation mechanisms into Indonesian judicial practice follows a six-stage methodology:

Observe: Identify systemic causes of low mediation success in Indonesian general civil courts (~4.0 percent), including solo mediator fatigue, lack of domain expertise, and absent evaluative tools.

Understand: Recognize that Japan achieves high settlement rates (>50 percent in general civil, >70 percent in inheritance) through multi-disciplinary Conciliation Committees (Chōtei Iinkai) and non-binding Orders in Lieu of Conciliation (Chōtei ni kawaru kettei).

Compare: Contrast Indonesia's solo mediator framework under PERMA 1/2016 against Japan's tripartite conciliation panels and Article 17 evaluative orders.

Adapt: Formulate specific regulatory amendments to PERMA No. 1 of 2016 under the JPAIS framework:

Establish Tripartite Conciliation Panels (Majelis Konsiliasi Tripartit) pairing one certified Judge Mediator with two accredited Non-Judge Expert Commissioners for commercial, property, and inheritance claims exceeding Rp 500 million.

Introduce an Order in Lieu of Settlement (Penetapan Pengganti Perdamaian), allowing panels to issue a provisional settlement decree that becomes a binding Settlement Deed (Akta Perdamaian) if no party objects within 14 calendar days.

Require immediate deposit of a security fee for non-appearance before adversarial pleadings can commence.

Pilot: Deploy a 90-day pilot across six target courts: PN Jakarta Pusat, PN Surabaya, PN Medan, PA Jakarta Selatan, PA Surabaya, and PA Malang.

Improve: Evaluate pilot outcomes against established targets: increase general civil court mediation success from ~4 percent to at least 25 percent, achieve an aggregate settlement rate of at least 60 percent in religious court property cases, and reduce average mediation duration from 30 working days to 21 calendar days or fewer.

## Judicial Knowledge Takeaways

Tripartite Panels Overcome Domain Knowledge Gaps: Pairing career judges with technical experts (accountants, land valuers, industry specialists) enhances credibility and facilitates interest-based negotiation.

Evaluative Settlement Orders Bridge Impasses: Empowering panels to issue provisional settlement orders subject to a 14-day objection window resolves deadlocks without violating party autonomy.

Mandatory Attendance Sanctions Prevent Dilatory Tactics: Enforcing financial deposits for non-attendance deters litigants from delegating mediation to representatives lacking settlement authority.

Targeted Pilot Testing Validates Procedural Reform: Deploying 90-day pilots across general and specialized courts generates empirical evidence to refine regulations before nationwide rollout.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is a Japanese Conciliation Committee (Chōtei Iinkai)? A: A Conciliation Committee under Articles 5 and 6 of the Civil Conciliation Act consists of one career judge (Chief Conciliator) and two lay Civil Conciliation Commissioners (Minji Chōtei-in) appointed from specialized civil professions.

Q: What is an Order in Lieu of Conciliation (Chōtei ni kawaru kettei) under Japanese law? A: Authorized by Article 17 of the Civil Conciliation Act, it is an ex-officio judicial order framing an equitable settlement when parties reach an impasse, gaining final judgment force if no objection is lodged within two weeks.

Q: What are the national mediation success rates in Indonesian general civil courts? A: Empirical data from Indonesian general civil courts (Pengadilan Negeri) indicates national mediation success rates between 4.0 percent and 4.08 percent.

Q: How does the proposed Order in Lieu of Settlement (Penetapan Pengganti Perdamaian) function for Indonesia? A: It allows a Tripartite Conciliation Panel to issue a provisional settlement order when negotiations deadlock, which converts into an enforceable Settlement Deed (Akta Perdamaian) unless a party objects within 14 calendar days.

## Japan Perspective

Judicial education in Japan is centralized under the Supreme Court of Japan (Saikō Saibansho) at the Legal Training and Research Institute (Shihō Kenshūjo) in Wako. Established in 1947, the Institute operates a unified professional pipeline where aspiring judges, public prosecutors (kenjetsukan), and private attorneys (bengoshi) undergo an identical 12-month post-bar apprenticeship.

The core analytical framework taught at Shihō Kenshūjo is the Requirements-Facts Doctrine (Yōken Jijitsu), developed by the Civil Trial Teachers Section (Minji Saiban Kyōkanshitsu). Yōken Jijitsu provides a standardized taxonomy that deconstructs private law claims into essential statutory elements (yōken jijitsu), facts establishing claims (seikyū-gen'in), defenses (kōben), and counter-defenses (reikōben), establishing a transparent burden of proof (kyoshō sekinin).

At the conclusion of the 12-month apprenticeship, trainees must pass the Second Examination (Nikai Shiken), a double-blind exit examination consisting of five 7.5-hour practical dossier tests covering Civil Judging, Criminal Judging, Prosecution, Civil Lawyering, and Criminal Defense. Under Article 43 of the Court Act (Saibansho-hō, Act No. 59 of 1947), newly appointed judges are designated as Assistant Judges (Hanjiho). Third, Indonesian candidate judges are appointed directly to single-judge dockets (Hakim Tunggal) in Class II District Courts immediately upon completing PPC Terpadu. In contrast, Japanese assistant judges undergo ten years of structured bench mentoring within three-judge panels (gōgi-sei).

Elemental Drafting Taxonomies Eliminate Reasoning Discrepancies: Deconstructing claims into statutory elements (Yōken Jijitsu / DFKUM) ensures concise judgments where every factual finding links directly to a statutory burden of proof.

Transitional Collegial Benches Protect First-Instance Adjudication: Restricting early-career judges to three-judge panels for initial service years prevents procedural errors and embeds clinical mentorship into daily court operations.

Dossier-Based Exit Exams Verify Analytical Readiness: Testing candidate judges on complex, anonymized trial dossiers (Nikai Shiken / UNKY) establishes an objective gateway before granting permanent judicial tenure.

Protected Mentorship Workloads Preserve Training Quality: Granting senior mentor judges formal caseload reductions ensures consistent, diagnostic feedback for candidate judges during court placements.

## Why This Topic Matters

The integration of artificial intelligence into judicial administration promises to streamline docket allocation, detect sentencing disparities, and improve legal research. However, deploying automated algorithms without transparent governance risks creating opaque decision-making, introducing systematic algorithmic bias, and infringing upon personal judicial independence (kemandirian hakim). ## Japan Perspective

Japan approaches artificial intelligence in judicial administration with institutional caution, prioritizing constitutional safeguards, data standardization, and transparent empirical methodologies over closed-box predictive algorithms.

Under Article 76 of the Constitution of Japan, judges are bound solely by the Constitution and statutory law, exercising their duties independently according to their conscience. The Supreme Court of Japan (Saikō Saibansho) maintains that core adjudicative functions—finding factual truth, interpreting statutory provisions, and determining criminal sentences—are personal duties of the judge that cannot be delegated to automated algorithms.

Rather than adopting predictive decision-making software, Japan focuses on building standardized, high-integrity digital infrastructure. Under the Act on Promotion of Civil Judicial Information Utilization (Act No. 49 of 2025), the judiciary systematically de-identifies, standardizes, and opens civil judgments for analytical processing.

For complex analytical tasks such as evaluating child support guidelines or assessing criminal sentencing ranges, Japan relies on transparent empirical studies conducted by the Legal Training and Research Institute (Shihō Kenshūjo). The resulting guidelines, such as the national child support matrix (santeihyō), are fully explainable, published openly, and subject to peer review across the legal profession.

COMPARATIVE PERSPECTIVE A comparative assessment between Japan and Indonesia highlights contrasting approaches to automated tools, data infrastructure, and algorithmic governance.

In Indonesia, the Supreme Court (Mahkamah Agung RI) has taken proactive steps to deploy artificial intelligence within court administration. Under its digital modernization agenda, the Supreme Court launched Smart Majelis, an automated application utilizing robotic algorithms to assign cases and select judicial panels across trial courts. Designed to enhance administrative transparency, prevent forum shopping, and mitigate corruption risks, Smart Majelis factors in judge caseloads, case classifications, and potential conflicts of interest.

However, key comparative differences emerge in governance and analytics focus:

First, Smart Majelis operates with unpublished algorithmic criteria, weightings, and decision parameters that are not currently subject to independent external audits. In contrast, Japan enforces strict explainability standards, prohibiting closed-box algorithms from impacting judicial administration or case handling.

Second, AI adoption in Indonesia remains concentrated on administrative case management tasks rather than substantive precedent analytics. Courts lack institutional tools to detect sentencing disparities or track appellate legal splits across regional jurisdictions.

Third, Indonesia currently lacks a formal Algorithmic Governance and Ethical Charter for Artificial Intelligence in the Judiciary to protect adjudicative independence under Law No. 48 of 2009 on Judicial Power.

Observe → Understand → Compare → Adapt → Pilot → Improve

The operational methodology for adapting Japanese AI governance and empirical research practices into Indonesian judicial reform follows six structured stages:

Observe: Identify governance gaps in Indonesian court automation, including unpublished algorithmic weightings in Smart Majelis and the absence of substantive precedent analytics tools for judges.

Understand: Recognize that Japan preserves judicial integrity by enforcing Article 76 constitutional guardrails, prioritizing structured open data under Act No. 49 of 2025, and utilizing fully explainable empirical studies (Shihō Kenshūjo).

Compare: Contrast Indonesia's closed-box administrative automation against Japan's transparent empirical guidelines and statutory de-identification framework.

Adapt: Formulate three regulatory and technical reforms under the JPAIS-AI framework for Mahkamah Agung RI:

Adopt the Supreme Court Code of Ethics and Algorithmic Governance for Artificial Intelligence in the Judiciary, prohibiting automated judicial determinations and mandating explainability.

Mandate independent algorithmic transparency audits for all court applications, including Smart Majelis.

Develop the Simetris Precedent Analytics Engine operated by Pustrajak Kumdil BSDK and Kepaniteraan MA as a strictly advisory decision-support tool that maps landmark precedents (putusan penting) and sentencing ranges without prescribing outcomes.

Pilot: Deploy a 90-day pilot testing the advisory Simetris Precedent Analytics Engine across the criminal chambers of PN Jakarta Pusat and PN Surabaya, specifically analyzing narcotics offense sentencing under Law No. 35 of 2009.

Improve: Evaluate pilot outcomes against established targets: achieve 100 percent explainability audit certification for internal algorithms (Smart Majelis and Simetris), maintain zero documented claims of automated encroachment on judicial discretion, and calibrate de-identification pipelines under SK KMA 2-144/2022 to protect personal privacy in training datasets.

## Judicial Knowledge Takeaways

Constitutional Guardrails Protect Adjudicative Autonomy: Codifying an absolute prohibition on automated judicial decision-making preserves the personal constitutional duty of judges to resolve disputes independently.

Algorithmic Transparency Builds Institutional Trust: Subjecting administrative automation tools to independent explainability audits prevents unaccountable code logic from disrupting court operations.

Clean Structured Data Precedes Predictive Analytics: Standardizing judgment metadata and automating privacy-compliant de-identification creates the necessary foundation for reliable legal research tools.

Advisory Decision Support Enhances Consistency: Providing judges with non-binding empirical summaries of historic sentencing ranges reduces unexplained regional disparities without infringing upon judicial discretion.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How does Article 76 of the Constitution of Japan regulate judicial AI? A: Article 76 mandates that judges are bound only by the Constitution and laws, exercising their duties independently according to their conscience. The Supreme Court interprets this as prohibiting the delegation of core adjudicative tasks to automated algorithms.

Q: What is Indonesia's Smart Majelis application? A: Smart Majelis is an automated application deployed by the Supreme Court of Indonesia that utilizes robotic algorithms to distribute cases and select judicial panels based on judge workloads and case classifications.

Q: What is the proposed Simetris Precedent Analytics Engine? A: Simetris is a proposed advisory decision-support tool operated by Pustrajak Kumdil BSDK that provides judges with non-binding comparative summaries of historic precedents and sentencing ranges.

Q: What statutory enactment governs civil judgment data utilization in Japan? A: The Act on Promotion of Civil Judicial Information Utilization (Act No. 49 of 2025) establishes institutional mechanisms to systematically de-identify, standardize, and open civil judgments for analytical processing.

Q: What are the primary performance targets for the JPAIS-AI pilot project? A: Targets include achieving 100 percent explainability audit certification for all court algorithms (Smart Majelis and Simetris) and recording zero instances of automated encroachment on judicial independence.
